subject: Post-call recap: throughput vs latency tradeoffs and reserved pool recommendation
messages:
From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood-inference.com>
To: Kevin Liu <kevin@neuroflux.ai>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood-inference.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>
Date: Tue, 19 May 2026 14:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap: throughput vs latency tradeoffs and reserved pool recommendation

Kevin—great conversation earlier. Quick recap and recommended next steps so we have a single source of truth. I captured what you emphasized on the call plus an initial recommended commitment and SLA posture for a reserved GPU pool.

Key pain points you reiterated:
- Latency-sensitive inference for user-facing features (95th perc target ~120–150ms token latency)
- Spiky traffic tied to business hours, but predictable weekly patterns (sustained daytime throughput, short high-concurrency bursts)
- Data isolation needs: PHI-adjacent payloads require tenant isolation and auditability

Goals we aligned on:
- Keep 95th token latency <=150ms for chat endpoints at target concurrency
- Avoid cold-start variability during bursts; prefer reserved capacity with short autoscale burst windows
- Instrumentation for token-level cost and per-route latency in Redwood Console

Recommended reserved pool (initial):
- Committed: 8x A100-class GPUs (reserved) to cover baseline throughput with continuous batching
- Burst: additional 4x on-demand GPUs for predictable high-concurrency windows (10–20 min bursts)
- Isolation: single-tenant pool with KV cache partitioning and role-based access; logs shipped to customer-managed S3 for compliance
- SLA: 99.9% availability for reserved pool; 2 hour RTO for failover to fallback model variant in a different region

Attached I’m including a short sizing workbook and a one-page recommendation PDF. Jordan and Ben are cc’d to add ops/implementation constraints and to schedule a tech scoping.

Next steps (asks):
1) Kevin: share an anonymized week of traffic (per-minute qps & typical sequence length distribution) — we’ll use it to refine sizing in the workbook (NeuroFlux export or summarized CSV).
2) Redwood (Jordan/Ben): provide a line-item estimate (OPEX) vs committed pricing and draft SLA language by EOD Wed.
3) Kevin/Contracts: flag any procurement cadence or security questionnaires we should expect (SOC2 artifacts, IP/exfiltration constraints).

If that aligns I’ll follow up with a tech scoping invite for early next week and a draft commercial worksheet.

Best,
Jonas
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
jonas.weber@redwood-inference.com | +1 (415) 555-9213

Attachments: redwood-reserved-pool-recommendation.pdf (PDF, 1 page), neuroflux-capacity-estimate.xlsx (spreadsheet)
From: Kevin Liu <kevin@neuroflux.ai>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood-inference.com>
Cc: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood-inference.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>, contracts@neuroflux.ai
Date: Tue, 19 May 2026 15:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: throughput vs latency tradeoffs and reserved pool recommendation

Thanks Jonas, that looks right and useful — appreciate the concise plan. A few clarifications from my side:

- The 95th token latency target is accurate; we measure user-facing latency end-to-end and want to keep model latency under ~120ms to preserve buffer for network UI latency.
- Bursts: typical burst events last 5–12 minutes, but we sometimes see back-to-back bursts across an hour during product launches.
- Isolation: yes, we need tenant isolation for any models that see PII/PHI. We can tolerate shared control plane as long as logs and keys are customer-owned.

I’ve attached a small sample export (aggregated minute-level qps + median sequence length). I’m sending the real CSV to Jordan’s shared drive link you included. Contracts is cc’d and will flag timeline constraints — we prefer a 30-day procurement window but we can be flexible on effective date.

Two asks from my side: can you call out expected token cost delta between committed vs burst instances (ballpark)? And, do you recommend quantized variants for the baseline to reduce cost without hurting quality?

Thanks — Kevin
Head of Platform Engineering | NeuroFlux
kevin@neuroflux.ai

Attachments: neuroflux_sample_20260518.zip (aggregated CSV inside)
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood-inference.com>
To: Kevin Liu <kevin@neuroflux.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood-inference.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>
Date: Wed, 20 May 2026 08:17:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: throughput vs latency tradeoffs and reserved pool recommendation

Kevin — thanks for the sample export, that helps. Quick notes from an ops/implementation viewpoint:

- Cost delta: committed GPUs (reserved) will reduce per-token OPEX by ~25–40% vs on-demand burst instances depending on sustained utilization and batching efficiency. I’ll add a worked example in the worksheet.
- Quantization: for NLP models with long-context conversational workloads we typically recommend mixed-precision (8-bit quantization on feed-forward + selective FP16 attention) as a starting point. That often yields 1.6–2.1x throughput improvement without measurable drop in top-level quality for ranking/generation tasks; we’ll A/B a quantized variant in canary.
- Autoscale policy suggestion: maintain baseline reservation for steady hours; enable instant burst pool warmup + pre-warming based on scheduled events (we can pre-warm 10 min before expected launches).

Operational asks for sizing: please confirm
1) 95th percentile request QPS target during peak hour (from your sample we have a range, choose the conservative top of the hour)
2) Typical mean & 95th sequence length (tokens) for chat endpoints
3) Any regulatory constraints that would require on-prem HSM for keys or restricted egress

I’ll update the workbook and SLA draft (attached) with these details and send a commercial worksheet for signoff later today. Jonas — I’ll defer pricing numbers to you but will include ops assumptions so the math is consistent.

-Jordan
Director, Solutions Architecture | Redwood Inference

Perfect — thanks Kevin and Jordan. We’ll incorporate the sample and follow up today with: a) a line-by-line committed pricing vs burst estimate, b) short SLA draft covering availability and failover, and c) a proposed kickoff date and mutual action plan (procurement -> security review -> implementation -> staged cutover).

Proposed immediate next step: 30-minute tech scoping on Mon 24 May at 10am PT (Jordan leading, Ben on ops) — Kevin, let me know if that works and whether you want a separate commercial call for procurement to join.

Jonas
